This appendix is non-normative. It highlights how this standard differs from RFC 3986 and +RFC 3987, and assumes familiarity with all three. [[RFC3986]] [[RFC3987]] + +

Most of these differences also produce a validation error, though in practice those are +seldom reported. + + + +

Different parsers

+ +

Under this standard, the following inputs parse differently than under RFC 3986 or RFC 3987: + +

    +

  • Non-ASCII input is percent-encoded rather than rejected. + https://example.com/café → https://example.com/caf%C3%A9. + +

  • Because non-file special schemes reject an empty host, extra slashes can + consume the input meant to be the path. http:///path → http://path/. + By contrast, file:///path parses as expected (empty host, path + "/path"). + +

  • Domain hosts of special URLs go through UTS #46 ToASCII, which converts Unicode labels + to Punycode and lowercases ASCII labels. https://☕.EXAMPLE/ → + https://xn--53h.example/. Non-special hosts are preserved verbatim. + +

  • IPv4 addresses accept octal, hexadecimal, and fewer-than-four parts, and are always + serialized as dotted-decimal. http://0x7f.1 → http://127.0.0.1/; + http://1.2.3 → http://1.2.0.3/. + +

  • Whether a host is IPv4 or a domain is decided by whether it ends in a numeric-looking + label. http://255.example parses as a domain; http://example.255 + fails. + +

  • The IPvFuture production is not recognized. + http://[v1.fe80]/ fails. + +

  • RFC 6874 IPv6 zone identifiers are not recognized. + http://[fe80::a%25eth0]/ fails. + +

  • A file: URL with host "localhost" normalizes to an empty host. + file://localhost/ → file:///. + +

  • file: URLs recognize Windows drive letters (normalizing U+007C (|) to + U+003A (:)) and preserve them across ... file:///C|/demo → + file:///C:/demo; .. against file:///C:/demo → + file:///C:/. + +

  • Percent-encoded dot segments always collapse as "."/"..". + /a/%2E%2E/b against http://example.com/ → + http://example.com/b. RFC 3986 only reaches the same result with optional + percent-encoding normalization. + +

  • http://example.com/%61 and http://example.com/a parse as + distinct URLs; RFC 3986's optional percent-encoding normalization would treat them as the + same. + +

  • A base URL with an opaque path supports only fragment-only + relative references. ?foo against bar:opaque fails; #foo + against the same yields bar:opaque#foo. + +

  • RFC 3986 non-strict reference resolution is used for special schemes only. + https:example.org against https://example.com/ → + https://example.com/example.org. + +

  • In an HTML document with a non-UTF-8 legacy encoding, the query of a special URL (other + than ws: or wss:) is percent-encoded using that encoding. + ?smörgåsbord in a windows-1252 document → query + sm%F6rg%E5sbord. + +

  • Leading and trailing C0 control or space are stripped from the input; interior + U+0009, U+000A, and U+000D are silently removed. + https://exa mp le.com/ (with a U+0009 between "exa" and + "mp" and a U+000A between "mp" and "le.com/") → + https://example.com/. + +

  • Out-of-grammar code points in the path, query, or fragment are percent-encoded rather + than rejected, and a bare U+0025 (%) is preserved. + https://example.org/foo bar → https://example.org/foo%20bar; + https://example.com/% parses distinctly from https://example.com/%25. +

+ + +

Different model
body:
I would lead with this section and make it stronger / change the framing. Something like:

> This standard is based around a parser and serializer, with a structured data type (the URL record) as the intermediary. RFC 3986 and RFC 3987 are based around ABNF grammars, which can be run against input strings to produce a boolean "matches / doesn't match" verdict. (In some cases, one can infer a decomposition of the input strings into substrings by looking at which sub-productions of the RFCs match which substrings of the input. But this is tricky to do consistently.)

Similarly, it may be worth mentioning how the URL Standard approaches normalization and relative URL resolution as something done during parsing, instead of having separate [Reference Resolution](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-5) and [Normalization and Comparison](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-6) steps (especially the complex multi-step comparison ladder). Although that touches on https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/729 and related issues.

body:
This bullet is inaccurate ("Non-special hosts are preserved verbatim") and less informative than it could be. Maybe something like

> Non-ASCII domain host treatment differs. Special URLs go through UTS \#\46's ToASCII, which converts Unicode labels to Punycode and lowercases ASCII labels: `https://☕.EXAMPLE/` → `https://xn--53h.example/`. Non-special URLs are percent-encoded: `foo://☕.EXAMPLE/` → `foo://%E2%98%95.EXAMPLE/`. This contrasts with 3986, which rejects non-ASCII hosts and only optionally lowercases them, or 3987, which suggests percent-encoding as a default with an older, buggier version to ToASCII from RFC 3490 as a fallback for an undefined set of schemes.

body:
Notable missing cases probably worth including:

- Port normalization (especially default-port elision and restriction to < 2^16)
- Host percent-*decoding*, e.g. parsing of `https://exam%70le.org/` and `https://exa%23mple.org/`.
- IPv6 normalization (similar to what is already mentioned for IPv4)
- Userinfo format; in particular the URL Standard splits at first `:` into username and password but the RFC deprecates the `username:password` format
- Allowing `@` in userinfo and percent-encoding it (i.e. `https://a@b@example.com/`)
- URL code points are a superset of 3987, e.g. `U+FFF0` is allowed by the URL Standard
- Scheme lowercasing
